title: Psalm 110: The King Who Is Also a Priest
summary: The LORD speaks to the psalmist's lord, inviting him to sit at God's right hand until his enemies are defeated, and sends his rule out from Zion. God swears an oath that this king is a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. The psalm ends with the Lord crushing kings in judgment and the king refreshed and lifting up his head.
story: Psalm 110 is the last of the three psalms of David (108 to 110) that open Book V. Psalm 109 ended with God standing at the right hand of the needy; Psalm 110 begins with a king invited to sit at God's right hand. For a community that no longer had a king on David's throne, a psalm about an enthroned son of David who reigns forever pointed ahead, and Jewish and Christian readers alike came to hear it as a promise about the Messiah, the anointed king to come. No psalm is quoted or echoed more often in the New Testament. It becomes the church's main text for saying that Jesus, raised from the dead, now reigns at the right hand of God.
historical:
The heading is “A Psalm of David.” Most scholars classify Psalm 110 as a royal psalm, a poem from Jerusalem's court, probably spoken at a king's enthronement, when a prophet or priest delivered God's word to the new ruler. Its Hebrew is old and difficult, which many take as a sign of an early date during the monarchy. A few scholars in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries dated it to the second century BC, when the Hasmonean rulers held the offices of both king and high priest, but that view has largely been abandoned. The traditional view, which Jesus assumes in his debate with the scribes (Mark 12:35-37), is that David himself spoke the psalm about a lord greater than himself. Many modern scholars read the heading as meaning a psalm for or about the Davidic king, composed by a court poet addressing the king as “my Lord.”

The mention of Melchizedek links the psalm to Jerusalem's past. In Genesis 14:18-20, Melchizedek is king of Salem and priest of God Most High, and he blesses Abraham. Psalm 76:2 uses Salem as a name for Jerusalem. When David captured Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5), he took over a city with a tradition of priest-kings. David did perform some priestly acts, such as wearing a linen ephod before the ark (2 Samuel 6:14), and 2 Samuel 8:18 even calls his sons priests, but the Davidic kings were not Levitical priests, and kings who overstepped priestly boundaries were judged (2 Chronicles 26:16-21).
cultural:
To sit at a king's right hand was to hold the place of highest honor and delegated power. Ancient Near Eastern kings are pictured in art with defeated enemies under their feet or serving as footstools, and a footstool was part of a royal throne; Tutankhamun's footstool, for example, was decorated with images of foreign captives. The scepter was the symbol of the king's authority, stretched out from Zion, the hill of the temple and palace in Jerusalem.

Verse 3 is one of the hardest verses in the Hebrew Bible to translate. The BSB speaks of a willing people, holy splendor, the womb of the dawn, and the dew of youth, all images of freshness and vigor at the king's accession. The ancient Greek translation, the Septuagint, read the same consonants differently and rendered the line as God saying that he had begotten the king from the womb before the morning star, which echoes Psalm 2:7. Verse 7 is also obscure. Some see a warrior refreshed at a stream in the middle of pursuit; others connect it with a coronation rite at a spring, since Solomon was anointed at the Gihon spring (1 Kings 1:38-40).
literary: The psalm is built around two divine oracles, each introduced by the LORD speaking. The first (verse 1) invites the king to sit at God's right hand; verses 2 and 3 expand it with the scepter going out from Zion and the people rallying. The second (verse 4) is an oath that he is a priest forever; verses 5 to 7 expand it with the day of wrath and the king's triumph. The first line uses a word normally found in prophecy, a solemn utterance of the LORD. There is also a play on titles: the LORD (God's name) speaks to “my Lord,” where the Hebrew is adoni, the ordinary word for a human master or king, and in verse 5 “The Lord” is Adonai, a title of God, who is now at the king's right hand. The psalm moves from throne to battlefield in only seven verses.

outline.t: First oracle: sit at my right hand
The scepter from Zion and a willing people
Second oracle: a priest forever like Melchizedek
The day of wrath and the king's triumph

doctrines.note: The psalm describes a king from David's line who shares God's throne, rules from Zion over his enemies, and holds a permanent priesthood by God's oath. The New Testament reads it as a portrait of Jesus the Messiah, and the creeds' confession that he is seated at the right hand of the Father comes from this verse.

God rules through his appointed king, and that rule advances even “in the midst of Your enemies.” The kingdom is not yet complete (the enemies are not yet a footstool), but it is established and certain.

Verse 4 joins kingship and priesthood in one person. The letter to the Hebrews builds on this to argue that Christ is a priest by God's oath, not by descent from Levi, and that his one sacrifice and endless life make his priesthood permanent.

words.note: Adon, lord or master, used of human superiors, including kings. In verse 1 the LORD speaks to adoni, “my lord.” Jesus' question in Mark 12 turns on this word: if David calls the Messiah his lord, how can the Messiah be merely his son? The title points to someone greater than David himself.

Kohen, priest. Priests in Israel came from the tribe of Levi and the family of Aaron, while kings came from Judah. Declaring the king a priest forever is therefore startling, and the psalm grounds it not in descent but in God's sworn oath and in the older order of Melchizedek.

Melchizedek, whose name means king of righteousness. He appears only here and in Genesis 14 in the Old Testament, as the king of Salem and priest of God Most High who blessed Abraham. Hebrews 7 reflects on his mysterious appearance without recorded ancestry as a picture of a priesthood with no beginning or end.

Shava, to swear an oath. God “has sworn and will not change His mind.” An oath makes a promise unbreakable, and Hebrews 7:20-22 argues that because Christ's priesthood rests on such an oath it is better and more secure than the Levitical priesthood, which had none.

christ: Psalm 110 is the Old Testament text most used by the New Testament to explain who Jesus is. Jesus himself asked how David could call the Messiah “my Lord” if the Messiah was David's son (Mark 12:35-37), implying that the Messiah is more than a human king. At Pentecost Peter quoted verse 1 to say that the risen Jesus has been exalted to God's right hand (Acts 2:34-36). Paul echoes it when he says Christ must reign until all his enemies are under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25), and Hebrews quotes both verse 1 and verse 4 to present Jesus as enthroned Son and eternal priest (Hebrews 1:13; 5:6; 7:17). Here the link is not only a matter of theme: the New Testament writers read the psalm as speaking directly of the Messiah, and the church's confession that Christ is seated at the right hand of the Father rests on it.

hard.q: Did David write this psalm about the Messiah, or is it a court poem about an ordinary king?
hard.a: Jesus' argument in Mark 12 assumes that David spoke the psalm and that “my Lord” refers to someone beyond David, and many Christian interpreters take that as settling the question: David, speaking by the Spirit, foresaw a descendant greater than himself. Many modern scholars read the psalm first as a coronation oracle composed for a king in Jerusalem, in which a court prophet calls the king “my Lord,” and they see the messianic reading as the way later Israel and the church rightly came to hear it once no king sat on David's throne. Some rabbinic interpreters applied the psalm to Abraham, because of the Melchizedek connection. These views need not be wholly opposed: a psalm first used for Davidic kings can promise more than any of them fulfilled, and the New Testament claims that Jesus is the one in whom the promise finally matches the person. Christians confess that fulfillment as a first-order truth, while holding the question of the psalm's original setting more openly.

questions: The king in this psalm sits and waits while God defeats his enemies. What does it mean for your own struggles that Christ reigns now, even while the enemies are not yet under his feet?
Jesus used verse 1 to press his hearers to think harder about who the Messiah is. How would you answer his question about how David's son can also be David's Lord?
Hebrews finds comfort in a priest who lives forever. What difference does it make to prayer that Christ is both king and priest?
